parsed.wine_summary:
Lafage is a Roussillon estate run by Jean-Marc and Eliane Lafage, a couple with serious technical credentials — Jean-Marc trained in viticulture and oenology and has consulted across multiple continents. Their Tessellae ('Vieilles Vignes' on the label) sits in the Côtes Catalanes IGP, a flexible designation covering 118 communes across the Pyrénées-Orientales that allows producers to work with old-vine material that doesn't fit neatly into the stricter Roussillon AOC rules. That flexibility matters here: the blend of Syrah, Carignan Noir, Grenache, and Monastrell reflects the actual diversity of old plantings in this part of southern France, where Monastrell (Mourvèdre's Spanish cousin) crossed the border long before appellations existed.

At 14.5% ABV across multiple vintages, this is a warm-climate wine — Roussillon is one of the sunniest and driest departments in France, averaging over 300 days of sunshine annually and regularly seeing the Tramontane wind, which desiccates grapes and concentrates sugars. The 'Vieilles Vignes' designation isn't legally defined in France, but in practice Lafage uses it to signal vines with root systems deep enough to access subsoil moisture and mineral complexity that younger plantings simply can't reach. The result is a wine with more structure and savory depth than the price suggests.

The climate is Mediterranean-continental, with cold winters, blazing summers, and the Tramontane wind acting as a natural disease suppressant — which means lower intervention in the vineyard and older vines that don't need to be replaced as often. At 14.5% alcohol, the ripeness is real, but old-vine Carignan and Grenache on schist hold onto acidity and savory garrigue character (thyme, black olive, dried herbs) that keeps the wine from reading as jammy. The tannins come primarily from Carignan and Syrah — firm but not harsh, with the kind of mineral backbone that schist-grown fruit tends to produce.

Without this step, old-vine Carignan can taste hard and rustic; with it, you get concentration and freshness simultaneously. The Syrah and Grenache are likely handled with more conventional vinification — destemming, temperature-controlled fermentation — to preserve structure and aromatics. Aging is in a combination of tank and older oak (Lafage's house style avoids heavy new oak on their entry-level and mid-tier wines), which keeps the fruit forward without burying the terroir under wood. The result across multiple vintages is a consistent 14.5% wine that drinks fuller than its price point implies.
parsed.food_pairing:
1. Merguez sausage with harissa and flatbread — the lamb fat, spice, and char are a natural match for Carignan's iron-and-herb character and the wine's warmth. The acidity cuts through the fat without fighting the spice.
2. Braised lamb shoulder with white beans and rosemary — a Catalan-style braise that mirrors the wine's garrigue notes (rosemary, thyme) and gives the tannins something substantial to grip.
3. Duck confit with lentils — the rendered duck fat and earthy lentils amplify the Syrah's dark fruit and the wine's savory depth; this is a classic Roussillon pairing for good reason.
4. Manchego and membrillo (quince paste) — the salty, slightly funky cheese and sweet-tart quince bridge the wine's fruit and savory elements; works as a casual cheese board anchor.
5. Grilled lamb kebabs with sumac yogurt — the acidity in the yogurt and the tartness of sumac echo the wine's mineral edge, while the char on the lamb plays to the Syrah and Monastrell components.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Domaine Gauby 'Vieilles Vignes' Côtes Catalanes — also old-vine Roussillon with schist terroir and Carignan in the blend, but Gauby sits at 3-4x the price; the comparison shows how much value Lafage extracts from similar raw material.
Les Vignes de Bila-Haut (Chapoutier) Côtes du Roussillon Villages — comparable price range, similar Mediterranean blend, but leans more on Grenache and Syrah than Carignan, giving it a slightly rounder profile with less of Tessellae's savory edge.
Chateau Pech-Latt Corbières — neighboring appellation, similar schist-and-limestone soils, Carignan-dominant blends at comparable prices; a useful benchmark for what old-vine southern French reds deliver at this tier.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry red with firm tannins, garrigue-driven savory depth, and dark fruit concentration from old-vine Mediterranean varieties
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through 2026-2027 for the 2013 and 2014 vintages; the 2009 is approaching its ceiling. Store at 55-60°F away from light. Decanting for 30-45 minutes opens up the Carignan's fruit and softens the tannins noticeably.
parsed.value_assessment: $14.56 at LCBO makes this one of the more honest value propositions in southern French reds at that price tier. Direct competitors include Chapoutier's Bila-Haut Côtes du Roussillon and Bonpas Côtes du Rhône, both of which trade blows with Tessellae on fruit but lack the old-vine complexity. At this price, you're getting schist-grown, vieilles vignes fruit from one of Roussillon's most technically proficient producers — it's worth buying by the case.
parsed.market_position: This wine lives on casual restaurant lists as a by-the-glass pour for tables that want something more interesting than a generic Côtes du Rhône, and on retail shelves as a reliable weeknight red for buyers who've graduated past entry-level Languedoc. It's not a collector's wine — the vintages available suggest Lafage produces it in volume — but it consistently punches above its price in blind tastings, which is why it keeps showing up in LCBO's portfolio. The audience is the informed casual drinker: someone who knows what Carignan is and why old vines matter, but isn't spending $30+ on a Tuesday.
parsed.insider_take: The Monastrell in this blend is the underrated piece — most people focus on Carignan's old-vine story or Syrah's aromatics, but Monastrell (which thrives just across the Spanish border in Jumilla) adds a dark, inky density and a slightly animal quality that gives Tessellae more grip than a typical Grenache-forward Roussillon blend. The tradeoff is that the wine can feel a touch heavy on its own; it really does need food. Skip it if you're looking for a light, easy-drinking red — but if you're sitting down to a lamb dish or a charcuterie spread, this is exactly the wine to open.
